import re


team_data = []

for year in range(2016,2027):
    url = f"https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_{year}_standings.html"
    data = requests.get(url)
    soup = bs(data.text, "html.parser")
    tables = soup.find_all("table")
    for table in tables:
        df = pd.read_html(str(table))[0]
        df["Year"] = year
        team_data.append(df)

    #^that above collected the team data from 2015 to the year listed in the paranthesis - 1, including standings.

teams_df = pd.concat(team_data,ignore_index=True)

cols = ["Western Conference"] + base_cols

def clean_team_name(t):
    if pd.isna(t):
        return t #means if its empty return it back but if not then ->
    t = str(t)
    
    t = re.sub(r"\*", "", t)
    t = re.sub(r"\(\d+\)", "", t)

    return t.strip()
  

east['Team'] = east['Team'].apply(clean_team_name) #we call the clean function and this cleans whatever we apply it top

text:
This is the MVP prediction machine — below are two different ways of ranking who’s having the best MVP case this season.


The first table uses my own custom MVP score, a weighted formula I built by hand that combines stats like points per game, assists per game, rebounds per game, team win percentage, and more. I chose the weights myself based on what I think matters most for an MVP case.


The second table uses a trained machine learning model instead. I trained a logistic regression model on 10 seasons of past MVP winners, so instead of me picking the weights, the model learned on its own which stats actually tend to separate MVP winners from everyone else. It then estimates each current player’s probability of winning MVP this season based on those learned patterns.


Comparing the two is part of the fun — sometimes they agree, sometimes they don’t, and the players ranked below are whoever came out on top in each method this season. There are also graphs further down showing how individual stats relate to MVP outcomes.
